1.pericope_label: The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof: when the eyes of man, as of all the tribes of Israel, shall be toward the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott reports that the opening place-name, long an insuperable difficulty, is now known from Assyrian inscriptions to have been a town near Damascus, and canvasses several renderings of the clause about the eye, preferring that the eyes of all will be turned to the Lord in wonder; Keil and Delitzsch treat the heading structurally, as marking this and a later oracle as corresponding portions of a greater whole.

Gill allows that the word rendered burden may also be a declaration or publication, the Arabic giving it as a revelation; Calvin insists on keeping the burden against those who render it prophecy, since the prophecy of the word would be strange and meaningless, and takes the doctrine as consolation to the godly, who are safe under one who wars against their enemies.

Clarke reproduces at length the argument that these chapters are not this prophet's and adds his own conclusion that they belong to a different and unknown author, and reports a rendering of the eye clause that the versions follow; Wesley takes the place-name for a Syrian city and country and reads the eye clause as the appeal of the wronged to heaven.

Henry presses the metaphor of the burden, a weight that those it rests on can neither shake off nor bear up under, admits that it does not appear why the country was so called, and draws a moral from each rendering of the eye clause.

debates.question: Should the heading be rendered burden or prophecy?

positions.position: Burden: the prophecy of the word would be strange and without meaning, whereas the burden of the word conveys a weight they cannot shake off.
It may be rendered a declaration or publication, the Arabic version making it a revelation.
A threatening proclamation of judgment, the same epithet marking two corresponding oracles.

debates.question: How should the clause about the eye be construed?

positions.position: The eye of man and of all the tribes will be directed to the Lord, so that when the judgments are fulfilled all turn to him in wonder.
The eye of the Lord is over man and over all the tribes; an easy sense that the versions follow.
Either, with a moral drawn from each.
Those wronged look to heaven for right.

outliers.claim: Sets out the case that these chapters were not written by the prophet whose name the book bears — that the earlier chapters are expressly assigned, connected and uniform in style while these are unassigned, unconnected, unsuitable in parts to the time, more adorned in composition, and break the unity of the book — and concludes that they form a distinct work by a different and unknown author.

themes: The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof: when the eyes of man, as of all the tribes of Israel, shall be toward the Lord.

2.pericope_label: And Hamath also shall border thereby; Tyrus, and Zidon, though it be very wise. And Tyrus did build herself a strong hold, and heaped up silver as the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets. Behold, the Lord will cast her out, and he will smite her power in the sea; and she shall be devoured with fire.

schools.summary: Ellicott concedes that the terms used of Syria are too general to fix an era but argues that the coastal city was certainly never burnt until Alexander, citing a historian's account of the houses fired after the slaughter, and refers the prophecy to that date; Keil and Delitzsch explain the syntax by which the northern city is tied to Damascus and separated from the pair that follows.

Gill describes the island city's natural and built defences and draws the double conclusion that it withstood neither Alexander nor the gospel, reports an ancient identification of the northern city with Antioch and finds a resting-place of the word there in the founding of a church, and gives the old Greek's reading by which the Lord inherits her.

Clarke argues that these prophecies suit an earlier prophet's day, since Damascus was taken without bloodshed and the coastal cities had lately been destroyed, and states that the prediction seems to have been fulfilled by the Babylonian rather than by Alexander; Wesley says the northern city was so near the storm it could not quite escape and takes the verb strictly, that she is cast out of her inheritance.

debates.question: By whom was the doom on these cities fulfilled?

positions.position: By Alexander: the city was never devoured with fire until his siege, and a detachment was sent against Syria at the same time.
By the Babylonian: Damascus was taken without bloodshed by Alexander, and the coastal cities had lately been destroyed and could hardly suffer again so soon.

debates.question: What does the verb rendered cast out mean?

positions.position: Cast out of her inheritance, which is what the word properly means.
The old Greek makes the Lord inherit her, so that converted she becomes his possession and her riches are devoted to his service.

outliers.claim: Reports an ancient identification of the northern city with Antioch and, if it holds, finds a resting-place of the word of the Lord there in a better sense, since the gospel was preached in that city, a church of Jews and Gentiles was formed, and the disciples were first called Christians there.

themes: And Hamath also shall border thereby; Tyrus, and Zidon, though it be very wise.
And Tyrus did build herself a strong hold, and heaped up silver as the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets.
Behold, the Lord will cast her out, and he will smite her power in the sea; and she shall be devoured with fire.

5.pericope_label: Ashkelon shall see it, and fear; Gaza also shall see it, and be very sorrowful, and Ekron; for her expectation shall be ashamed; and the king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited. And a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines. And I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth: but he that remaineth, even he, shall be for our God, and he shall be as a governor in Judah, and Ekron as a Jebusite. And I will encamp about mine house because of the army, because of him that passeth by, and because of him that returneth: and no oppressor shall pass through them any more: for now have I seen with mine eyes.

schools.summary: Ellicott fills in what the histories omit about the march, canvasses three views of the comparison with the Jebusite and prefers the one that makes them equals rather than a conquered race, resists tying the phrase about passing and returning to that march, and admits that nothing is known of any great conversion of Philistines at this time; Keil and Delitzsch state the turn plainly, that while the heathen world falls under judgment its remnant is converted and the Lord protects his house.

Gill makes the fear imitation and then conversion, supports it by a bishop of the place sitting in the great council, canvasses three identifications of the bastard, and takes the army for the persecutors who rose against the church in the first ages.

Clarke uses the fulfilment of these verses for his authorship argument, commits to Alexander as the bastard on the strength of his mother's story, takes the blood as the Philistines abstaining once incorporated with Israel, and refers the encamping to the conqueror met by the high priest in his robes; Wesley takes the bastard for strangers with no right of inheritance and keeps both the delight in blood and the abominable sacrifices.

debates.question: Who is the bastard that dwells in Ashdod?

positions.position: Alexander, whose mother told a story of a god entering her apartment in the shape of a dragon; the word signifies a stranger.
Not a person but a mixed race, connected with a policy of breaking up nationalities and fusing peoples.
Strangers, who have no right of inheritance.
Undecided among the name of a people, Alexander, and the Maccabean leader who burnt the place.

debates.question: What is meant by comparing Ekron to a Jebusite?

positions.position: The people who dwelt with Judah in Jerusalem as equals and not as a conquered race, since the word stands parallel with the term for governor.
As an inhabitant of Jerusalem, many Philistines having become proselytes.
The city put for the people, all the remaining Philistines becoming servants to the people of God.

outliers.claim: Remarks on the closing clause that in the estimation of the man of little faith God only sees when he actively interferes.

themes: Ashkelon shall see it, and fear; Gaza also shall see it, and be very sorrowful, and Ekron; for her expectation shall be ashamed; and the king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited.
And a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.

And I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth: but he that remaineth, even he, shall be for our God, and he shall be as a governor in Judah, and Ekron as a Jebusite.

And I will encamp about mine house because of the army, because of him that passeth by, and because of him that returneth: and no oppressor shall pass through them any more: for now have I seen with mine eyes.

9.pericope_label: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass. And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off: and he shall speak peace unto the heathen: and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the epithets as saved and afflicted, notes that the Hebrew is literally of she-asses and that riding so no longer denoted rank, argues that the deliberate performance of the act does not lessen its value as a fulfilment, and infers from the wording's source that the nation was to enjoy political independence with its military power ended; Keil and Delitzsch argue from the structure that a kingdom whose king comes without earthly exaltation will not be established by worldly power.
Gill takes the daughter addressed for the church and true believers rather than the inhabitants or the children in the temple courts, and asks a spiritual rather than an external rejoicing.

Clarke argues negatively that no king but Jesus has ruled that people since the last of the old dynasty, and explains the ass by the standing command against multiplying horses, which a mounted entry would have broken; Wesley glosses the epithets and says the king will need no external force, since neither chariot nor bow brought salvation to him.

Henry rests the identification on the literal accomplishment recorded in two Gospels, enlarges on the title of king, and records a rendering by which the king is saving himself, rising from the grave by his own power.

debates.question: How should the epithets of the coming king be rendered?

positions.position: Better saved and afflicted than having salvation and lowly.
He has salvation in his power to bestow, though some render it as saving himself.
He alone saves from sin and death.

debates.question: Why does the king ride an ass?

positions.position: Because the kings were commanded not to multiply horses, so a mounted entry would have broken a positive command.
Not to symbolise peace or humility, which cannot be proved, but to indicate an absence of pomp and worldly display.

outliers.claim: Argues that our Lord deliberately performed the act in view of this prophecy as a symbolic correction of false notions about the Messiah's mission, and that the deliberation does not lessen its value as a fulfilment, since any man might have ridden in on an ass but not amid the acclamations of a multitude whose hearts were already won, nor could any man have founded an almost universal religion.

themes: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.

And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off: and he shall speak peace unto the heathen: and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.

11.pericope_label: As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water. Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I declare that I will render double unto thee; When I have bent Judah for me, filled the bow with Ephraim, and raised up thy sons, O Zion, against thy sons, O Greece, and made thee as the sword of a mighty man.

schools.summary: Ellicott would render the stronghold as the steepness of their own land and reads the exhortation as addressed to those still in Babylon, supporting the setting from an earlier chapter admitted to postdate the return, and notes that the verbs of the following verse should be future, the tense being the prophetic perfect; Keil and Delitzsch supply the verses without comment.

Gill argues from the gender that the eleventh verse is addressed to the congregation and not to Christ, rejects the reading that makes the prisoners those who stayed in Babylon since they were at liberty to leave, and takes the bow spiritually as the apostles whose ministrations struck the hearts of men.

Clarke takes the covenant historically and the pit as the whole human race under the arrest of God's judgments, turns the stronghold into an appeal to conscience, and breaks with the others on the target of the bow, holding the language too strong for the Maccabean advantage and still to be fulfilled; Wesley makes the words Christ's own to Jerusalem and keeps the bow military and Maccabean.

Henry holds both readings of the prisoners together, the returned exiles prisoners in effect and those who stayed prisoners in fact, and directs both to the Messiah set before them in the promise as the stronghold of the faithful long before his coming.

debates.question: Whose words are addressed to Zion, and who are the prisoners?

positions.position: The Father's words to the church, the prisoners being those waiting for the consolation of Israel rather than those who stayed in Babylon at liberty to leave.
Christ's own words to Jerusalem, the pit being Babylon.
Addressed to those still remaining in Babylon and urged to come forth, prisoners still and prisoners of hope.
Both: the returned exiles prisoners in effect and those who stayed prisoners in fact.

debates.question: Against whom are the bow and arrows drawn?

positions.position: Against no earthly enemy: the bow is the apostles, whose ministrations brought men into subjection to Christ.
Against the Greeks, fulfilled in the Maccabean triumphs.
Not against them: the language is too strong for that trifling advantage and probably remains to be fulfilled against the present possessors of those countries.

outliers.claim: Would render the word usually given as stronghold rather as the steepness of their own land, and supports the exilic setting by quoting an earlier chapter of the book which is admitted on all sides to have been written after the return.

themes: As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water.
Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I declare that I will render double unto thee;
When I have bent Judah for me, filled the bow with Ephraim, and raised up thy sons, O Zion, against thy sons, O Greece, and made thee as the sword of a mighty man.

14.pericope_label: And the Lord shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth as the lightning: and the Lord God shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south. The Lord of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and subdue with sling stones; and they shall drink, and make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers that on their behalf God shall manifest himself, explains the quarter named as that of the most violent storms, would render that they trample on sling stones in their onslaught rather than subdue with them, and says the filling is with the blood of their enemies; Keil and Delitzsch keep to the sequence of promises and note that the verb rendered save cannot mean merely to help.

Gill lays out three renderings of the appearing, referring them to the days of Christ's flesh, to the ascension and Pentecost, and to protection given, and reads the defending spiritually as a shield over the apostles.

Clarke reads the appearing as a shadowing like the cloud over the camp, claims a discovery about the recurved bow and the kindling arrow that he says has escaped every commentator, and denies expressly that any drinking of enemies' blood is intimated; Wesley makes the arrow the divine judgments and takes the drinking as festival thanksgiving.

debates.question: What is the drinking and filling in the fifteenth verse?

positions.position: A victory feast on the spoils, with libations of wine poured at the altar; there is no intimation of drinking enemies' blood, as some barbarous nations did.
A filling with the blood of their enemies, like the bowls in which priests caught the victims' blood.
Drinking at festivals of thanksgiving and filling with the blood of the sacrifices offered.

debates.question: How should the appearing over them be rendered?

positions.position: Three ways: appearing to them, over and upon them, or for them.
Perhaps better, on their behalf shall he manifest himself.
A shadowing and refreshing, as the cloud over the camp in the wilderness.

outliers.claim: Claims a discovery that has escaped every commentator: the oriental bow must be bent backwards to be strung, so that one tribe is the recurved bow and the other the arrow laid on the string, discharged with the momentum of lightning and kindling in its course through the air.

themes: And the Lord shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth as the lightning: and the Lord God shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south.

The Lord of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and subdue with sling stones; and they shall drink, and make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar.

16.pericope_label: And the Lord their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people: for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land. For how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty! corn shall make the young men cheerful, and new wine the maids.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the word and idea of a flock enter here for the first time and go on to dominate the following chapters, says the possessive in the last verse means Israel's, and would render goodliness for goodness and making to grow numerously for making cheerful; Keil and Delitzsch render the closing promise that corn will make youths to sprout and read the possessive as the land's.

Gill applies the saving to those converted and subdued by the apostles' preaching, and denies that the goodness is of the land or of the law or of the people, taking it of the Messiah and of his goodness as Mediator rather than his essential or providential goodness.

Clarke renders the crowned stones as erecting themselves, allows that they may be stones anointed with oil, and extends the guess to the upright stones of his own country; Wesley reduces the same phrase to precious in my sight and the ensign to a trophy.

debates.question: Whose goodness and beauty does the last verse celebrate?

positions.position: The Messiah's, and not his essential or providential goodness but his goodness as Mediator.
Israel's: the pronoun means the nation's, and the word is better rendered goodliness.
Both directions at once, the goodness in himself and towards them, the beauty put in them and upon them.

debates.question: What are the stones of a crown?

positions.position: Crowned stones erecting themselves as monuments of a deliverance, or stones anointed with oil as a temporary altar for a victory.
Simply that they are precious in God's sight, the ensign being a trophy.

outliers.claim: Extends the crowned-stones reading to the antiquities of his own country, suggesting that most of the upright stones standing in circles which pass for druidical monuments were erected to commemorate victories or to grace the tomb of an illustrious chief.

themes: And the Lord their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people: for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land.
For how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty! corn shall make the young men cheerful, and new wine the maids.
